title: How to Choose a UV Light for Your HVAC System
h1: How to Choose a UV Light for Your HVAC System
description: Choose a UV light for your HVAC system by comparing coil and air units, lamp placement, replacement schedule and safety. What UV can and can't do for air.
quick_answer: Most homes do best with a coil-sterilization UV light installed near the AC coil, which keeps mold and bacteria from growing on the damp coil and drain pan. Air-sterilization lights in the ductwork target germs in moving air. Choose a UVC lamp sized for your system, avoid ozone-producing bulbs, and plan to replace the lamp on the manufacturer's schedule.
body:
What does a UV light in an HVAC system do?

HVAC UV lights use ultraviolet-C (UVC) light to damage the DNA of mold, bacteria and some viruses so they can't grow and multiply. The light is mounted inside the air handler or ductwork, where it's hidden from view.

The biggest benefit is keeping the AC coil and drain pan clean. These parts stay damp during cooling, which makes them a natural spot for mold and bacteria. A clean coil also transfers heat better and helps prevent musty smells.

What's the difference between coil and air UV lights?

Coil sterilization lights are installed near the evaporator coil and usually run all the time. Because they shine constantly on the same surfaces, they're very effective at keeping the coil and drain pan free of growth. For most homes, this is the type we recommend first.

Air sterilization lights are installed in the supply or return duct and treat air as it moves past. Air moves quickly, so the exposure time is short. These units usually run only when the blower is on and need more intensity to have an effect.

Some systems use both. Whether that's worth it depends on your goals and your budget.

What should you look for when choosing a UV light?

  • Compatibility. The light must fit your air handler or duct and run on the right voltage. Furnaces in tight attics and closets may limit where it can go.
  • UVC wavelength. Germicidal lamps typically operate around 254 nanometers, which is effective against microbes.
  • Ozone-free lamps. Some UV bulbs produce ozone, which can irritate the lungs. Choose lamps labeled ozone-free.
  • Lamp size and number. Larger coils may need a longer lamp or two lamps for full coverage.
  • Safety features. Look for door interlock switches that shut off the lamp when the cabinet is opened, and a viewing port that shows the lamp is working.
  • Replacement lamps. Make sure lamps are easy to buy, and check how long each one is rated to last.

What won't a UV light do?

UV lights don't remove dust, pollen, pet dander or smoke particles. Those need a good filter or air purifier. UV also won't fix a moisture problem. If your drain line is clogged or ducts are sweating in the attic, those issues need repair first.

Think of UV as one piece of a cleaner system, working alongside a good filter, clean ducts and proper humidity control.

Who benefits most from an HVAC UV light?

  • Homes with musty smells when the AC runs
  • Systems that have had mold on the coil or in the drain pan
  • Coastal homes where humid air keeps the coil damp for long periods
  • Households with mold-sensitive allergies or asthma
  • Homes with heavy AC use during hot inland summers

Should you install a UV light yourself?

We don't recommend it. Installation involves cutting into the air handler or duct and wiring the light into the system's electrical supply. UVC light can also burn eyes and skin with direct exposure. A technician will place the lamp for full coil coverage and add the safety interlock.

Our indoor air quality service installs and services UV lights, and we'll check the coil and drain pan while we're there.

How do you maintain a UV light?

UV lamps lose strength over time, even when they still glow. Most manufacturers recommend replacing the lamp on a set schedule, often every year or two. Lamps also collect dust, which blocks the light, so they should be wiped during maintenance.

The easiest approach is to have the lamp checked and cleaned at each tune-up and replaced when the manufacturer says it's due.

Write the install date on a label near the air handler or keep it with your service records. Since you can't see the lamp from the living area, a date is the simplest way to know when a replacement is coming up. If the viewing port ever shows the lamp is dark, call to have it checked rather than opening the cabinet yourself.
faqs: Do HVAC UV lights really work?

Coil UV lights are effective at keeping mold and bacteria from growing on the AC coil and drain pan. Air-sterilization lights help less, since moving air passes the lamp quickly. Neither removes dust or pollen.
How often should the UV lamp be replaced?
Most lamps need replacing every year or two, depending on the manufacturer. They lose germicidal strength over time even if they still light up.
When properly installed inside the air handler with safety interlocks and ozone-free lamps, they're safe for the home. Never look directly at a UVC lamp.
Will a UV light help with musty smells?
It often helps if the smell comes from mold or bacteria on the coil or drain pan. If the odor comes from ducts, the attic or a moisture leak, those need to be addressed directly.
